lines.say: Here's a question. Can you make a perfect copy of a qubit?
C NOT does it for plain zeros and ones, with a blank qubit set to zero.
It flips the blank only when the original is one, so zero gives zero zero, and one gives one one.
It's like a photocopier that only understands black and white.
A white page gives two white pages, and a black page gives two black ones.
But feed it a grey page, and it doesn't make a grey copy.
It binds the two pages together, so whenever anyone looks, both are black or both are white.
Now feed C NOT the plus state, an arrow lying flat on the equator.
Two true copies would give all four results, one time in four each.
Instead you only ever get zero zero or one one, half the time each.
They're entangled, their answers locked together, and neither has an arrow of its own.
That's not C NOT's fault. The no cloning theorem says no circuit can copy an unknown state.
With lots of copies, you could measure each along a different direction and work out the arrow.
But measuring one qubit only ever gives you one bit. Copying would sneak past that.
That's where the photocopier breaks. Anyone can see grey, but nobody can see a qubit's shade.
You can still make many qubits in a known state, though. Just repeat the recipe.
So no circuit copies an unknown state. C NOT copies zero and one, but entangles everything in between.
